doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Residuals and special payments
summary: He explains yearly special payments checks, game show jingle residuals, and a telethon rerun the union caught.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Are you a guy who gets random checks in the mail for things that you did in the past?

Yeah, yeah. Jingles that they might re-use. TV shows you don’t get residuals. Most of the stuff you do not receive residuals, not quarterly or anything, you get a yearly check and they total up what you did on records every August I think and they send you a check. It

could be a penny, it could be $40,000. It depends on how many records you’re on. And then they do the same thing for films. They’re called special payments. And the guys who have been in Los Angeles a while who really are into that, that fell into that, were very lucky fortunately. They could get checks for 50, 60, 70 thousand dollars every year. And then other guys could get checks for $200 every year. So yeah, special payments funds. And I did a lot of game show jingles at one point. That you get paid every — the musicians get checks for every six months I believe. So we get some residual things but it’s mostly the yearly special payments checks.
Would you know if you were getting or not getting something that you should? How the heck do you keep track of that?

No, I remember once I did a big telethon, one of the telethons, back in the 80s, and for some reason they re-ran this thing three days after it ended. And it was never done before like that. And one of the 80 musicians who were in the orchestra saw it and called up the union. And the union didn’t even know. So they got on it and we got paid 100 percent again. But you really wouldn’t know. There are supposedly librarians who keep track of all that, who work for the union or the TV show, and every time a station, like NBC or ABC or whatever station, releases music for something that people have recorded that the librarian fills out a cue sheet and sends that to ASCAP or BMI. Now there it goes through channels and whenever that happens, you never know, and then BMI or ASCAP takes care of cutting the musicians a check. But things could go over their heads, you know, the librarians, and they might not submit something. So there are instances where it happens. I don’t think it happens often. I think they’re pretty good at that.
